hello.title: Hello, COBOL!
hello.summary: Write your first COBOL program, learn how its divisions fit together and print text with DISPLAY.
hello.lesson.0: COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language) is one of the oldest programming languages. Banks, insurance companies and governments still run large COBOL programs every day. COBOL code reads almost like English sentences.
hello.lesson.2: The first line, `>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE`, tells the compiler that you use **free format**: a line may start in any column. Older COBOL code uses fixed format, where some columns have special meanings. This course always uses free format.
hello.lesson.3: `IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.` starts the first part of the program. `PROGRAM-ID. HELLO.` gives the program its name, here `HELLO`. `PROCEDURE DIVISION.` starts the part with the **statements**, the instructions that the computer runs from top to bottom.
hello.lesson.4: `DISPLAY` prints text and then ends the line. Text in double quotes, like `"Hello, COBOL!"`, is a **literal**: COBOL prints it exactly as written. `STOP RUN` ends the program.
hello.lesson.6: A COBOL program has up to four **divisions**, always in this order: `IDENTIFICATION`, `ENVIRONMENT`, `DATA` and `PROCEDURE`. Only the `IDENTIFICATION DIVISION` with `PROGRAM-ID` is required. You do not need the `ENVIRONMENT DIVISION` in this course, and you meet the `DATA DIVISION` in the next unit.
hello.lesson.8: One `DISPLAY` can print several items. It puts them next to each other without spaces, so you add spaces inside the quotes yourself. Numbers like `42` need no quotes. Each `DISPLAY` prints one line.
hello.lesson.10: Add `WITH NO ADVANCING` to stay on the same line. The next `DISPLAY` then continues where the last one stopped.
hello.lesson.12: The period `.` ends every division header and the `PROGRAM-ID` line. In the `PROCEDURE DIVISION`, this course puts a period only after the last statement, `STOP RUN.`. COBOL ignores upper and lower case in keywords, so `display` works like `DISPLAY`, but most COBOL code is written in capitals.
hello.lesson.13: In exercises, short examples often show only the statements of the `PROCEDURE DIVISION`. Imagine them inside a complete program like the ones above.
hello.card.0: `>>SOURCE FORMAT FREE` lets lines start in any column
hello.card.3: `DISPLAY "Total: " 42` prints items side by side and ends the line
hello-1.prompt: Which division holds the statements that the program runs?
hello-1.explain: The statements, such as `DISPLAY` and `STOP RUN`, always go into the `PROCEDURE DIVISION`.
hello-2.explain: `DISPLAY` prints its items next to each other without spaces and without the quotes.
hello-3.prompt: How many lines does this print?
hello-3.explain: `WITH NO ADVANCING` keeps `Two` on the same line as `One`. `Three` goes on the second line.
hello-4.explain: The three items are printed side by side. The spaces come from inside the quotes.
hello-5.statement: The `DATA DIVISION` may come before the `IDENTIFICATION DIVISION`.
hello-5.explain: The divisions always come in the same order, and `IDENTIFICATION DIVISION` is first.
hello-6.explain: COBOL ignores upper and lower case in keywords. Only the text inside quotes is printed exactly as written.
hello-7.prompt: Complete the program so it prints Hello.
hello-7.explain: COBOL prints with `DISPLAY`. `WRITE` exists, but it writes to files.
hello-8.prompt: Complete the line that ends the program.

hello-9.explain: `WITH NO ADVANCING` comes after the items, so the line does not end.

hello-10.explain: First the `IDENTIFICATION DIVISION` with the `PROGRAM-ID`, then the `PROCEDURE DIVISION` with the statements. `STOP RUN` comes last.

data.title: Data and PIC clauses
data.summary: Declare data items in WORKING-STORAGE, describe them with PIC clauses, give them start values and copy data with MOVE.
data.lesson.0: A program keeps values in **data items**, which other languages call variables. In COBOL you declare every data item before you use it. Data items go into the `DATA DIVISION`, in the `WORKING-STORAGE SECTION`, between the `IDENTIFICATION DIVISION` and the `PROCEDURE DIVISION`.
data.lesson.2: Each declaration is one line that ends with a period. `01` is the **level number**: `01` means a data item of its own. Then comes the name, which may use letters, digits and hyphens. `PIC` (short for picture) describes what the item can hold, and `VALUE` gives it a start value.
data.lesson.3: In a `PIC` clause, `9` stands for one digit, `X` for any character and `A` for a letter or a space. A number in parentheses repeats the character: `9(4)` is the same as `9999`, and `X(5)` holds exactly five characters.
data.lesson.4: The size is fixed. A number always shows all its digits, so `PIC 9(3)` with the value `7` prints `007`. Text that is shorter than its item is filled with spaces on the right. The brackets in the next example only show where the item starts and ends.
data.lesson.7: `MOVE 25 TO AGE` puts `25` into `AGE` and replaces the old value. `MOVE OLD-AGE TO AGE` copies the value of `OLD-AGE` into `AGE`, and `OLD-AGE` keeps its value. One `MOVE` can fill several items: `MOVE 0 TO A B`.
data.lesson.9: When a value is too big for its item, COBOL cuts it off without an error. Text loses characters on the **right**. Numbers lose digits on the **left**, because COBOL keeps the digits that line up with the item.
data.lesson.11: Higher level numbers such as `05` build a **group**: the `05` items belong to the `01` item above them. The group is all of its items in a row, so `DISPLAY PERSON` prints both parts without a space. A group has no `PIC` of its own.
data.lesson.13: From now on, short examples in exercises show the data items and the statements together. Imagine the `01` lines in the `WORKING-STORAGE SECTION` and the statements in the `PROCEDURE DIVISION`, followed by `STOP RUN`.
data.card.1: `01 AGE PIC 99 VALUE 18.` = level, name, picture, start value
data.card.4: Too big: text is cut on the right, numbers on the left
data-1.explain: `PIC 9(4)` always shows four digits, so COBOL adds two zeros on the left.

data-2.explain: `X` holds any character and `X(10)` has room for ten of them. `PIC X` holds only one character, and `9` is meant only for digits.
data-3.explain: `TOWN` has room for five characters. Text is cut off on the right.
data-4.explain: `YY` has two digits. Numbers lose their digits on the left, so `25` stays.
data-5.statement: `PIC 9(3)` and `PIC 999` describe the same kind of data item.
data-5.explain: The number in parentheses repeats the character, so `9(3)` means three digits, like `999`.

data-12.explain: `PIC 99` holds at most `99`, so the start value `100` does not fit. Use `PIC 999`.
arithmetic.title: Arithmetic
arithmetic.summary: Calculate with ADD, SUBTRACT, MULTIPLY, DIVIDE and COMPUTE, and work with decimals and ROUNDED.
arithmetic.lesson.0: COBOL has an English verb for each kind of calculation. `ADD 5 TO TOTAL` adds `5` to `TOTAL` and stores the result in `TOTAL`. `SUBTRACT 3 FROM TOTAL` subtracts. `MULTIPLY 2 BY TOTAL` and `DIVIDE 4 INTO TOTAL` also store their result in `TOTAL`, the last item.
arithmetic.lesson.2: With `GIVING`, the result goes into another item and the inputs stay the same. `DIVIDE A BY B GIVING C` divides `A` by `B`. Add `REMAINDER R` to keep what is left over.
arithmetic.lesson.5: `COMPUTE` calculates a whole formula and stores the result in the item before `=`. It uses `+` and `-`, `*` to multiply, `/` to divide and `**` for a power. `*` and `/` come before `+` and `-`, and parentheses change the order.
arithmetic.lesson.7: Always put spaces around the operators. A hyphen can be part of a name, so COBOL reads `A-B` as one name, not as `A` minus `B`. Write `A - B`.
arithmetic.lesson.9: `V` in a picture marks where the decimal point is. `PIC 9(3)V99` holds three digits before the point and two after it. The point is not stored, so to print the number nicely you move it to an **edited** picture. In an edited picture, `.` prints the point and `Z` prints a space instead of a leading zero.
arithmetic.lesson.11: If a result has more decimals than the item can hold, COBOL cuts the extra digits off. Add `ROUNDED` after the result item to round instead: `2.5` becomes `3`.
arithmetic.lesson.13: A result that is too big loses its digits on the left without an error: `99 + 1` in `PIC 99` gives `00`. Add `ON SIZE ERROR` and a statement to react instead, for example `ADD 1 TO N ON SIZE ERROR DISPLAY "Too big" END-ADD`. Then `N` keeps its old value.
arithmetic.card.0: `ADD 5 TO N`, `SUBTRACT 3 FROM N`, `MULTIPLY 2 BY N`, `DIVIDE 4 INTO N`
arithmetic.card.1: `DIVIDE A BY B GIVING C REMAINDER R`
arithmetic.card.2: `COMPUTE C = (A + B) * 2 ** 3` with spaces around operators
arithmetic.card.4: `COMPUTE N ROUNDED = 10 / 4` rounds instead of cutting
arithmetic-1.explain: `ADD 5 TO N` adds `5` to `7` and stores `12` in `N`.
arithmetic-2.explain: `17` divided by `5` is `3`, and `2` is left over.
arithmetic-3.explain: Without `GIVING`, `MULTIPLY 3 BY N` stores the result `12` in `N`.
arithmetic-5.explain: `7 / 2` is `3.5`. `Y` has no decimals, and `ROUNDED` rounds `3.5` up to `4`. Without `ROUNDED`, you get `3`.
arithmetic-6.explain: Each `Z` prints a space instead of a leading zero. The item still has three characters.
arithmetic-7.statement: This program stops with an error because the result does not fit.
arithmetic-7.explain: COBOL cuts the result `100` to the two digits `00` and goes on. Use `ON SIZE ERROR` to notice it.
arithmetic-8.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 12.
arithmetic-8.explain: `GIVING TOTAL` stores the result in `TOTAL` and leaves `PRICE` and `QTY` as they are.
arithmetic-9.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 025, the square of SIDE.
arithmetic-9.explain: `**` is the power operator: `5 ** 2` is `25`. `SIDE * 2` would give `10`.
arithmetic-10.prompt: Build the statement that subtracts 4 from TOTAL.
arithmetic-10.explain: `SUBTRACT` names the amount first and the item after `FROM`.
arithmetic-11.explain: COBOL reads `A-B` as one name. Put spaces around the minus: `COMPUTE C = A - B`.

conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Let the program choose with IF, ELSE and EVALUATE, and give values readable names with level 88.
conditions.lesson.0: `IF` runs statements only when a condition is true. `ELSE` adds statements for the other case, and `END-IF` closes the `IF`. Indent the statements inside so that you can see what belongs together.
conditions.lesson.2: You can compare with `=`, `>`, `<`, `>=`, `<=` and `NOT =` (not equal). COBOL also accepts words, such as `IS GREATER THAN` and `IS EQUAL TO`. `AND` needs both conditions to be true, `OR` needs at least one, and `NOT` turns a condition around.
conditions.lesson.4: Do not put a period inside an `IF`. A period ends the whole sentence, so it also ends the `IF`, and the next `ELSE` becomes an error. Close every `IF` with `END-IF` instead.
conditions.lesson.6: `EVALUATE` compares one item with several values. Each `WHEN` names a value, and `WHEN OTHER` catches everything else. COBOL runs only the first `WHEN` that matches and then continues after `END-EVALUATE`.
conditions.lesson.8: `WHEN 3 THRU 5` matches every value from `3` to `5`. With `EVALUATE TRUE`, each `WHEN` holds a full condition, and the first true one wins.
conditions.lesson.11: A level `88` item gives a value of the item above it a name. With `88 IS-RED VALUE "R"`, the condition `IF IS-RED` means `IF LIGHT = "R"`. `SET IS-GREEN TO TRUE` moves the value of `IS-GREEN` into `LIGHT`. A level `88` item can also list several values or a range with `THRU`.
conditions.lesson.13: Condition names make code easier to read: `IF IS-WEEKEND` explains itself, `IF DAY-NUM > 5` does not. Use them for values that have a meaning in your program.
conditions.card.0: `IF A > B ... ELSE ... END-IF`, no period inside
conditions.card.2: `EVALUATE X WHEN 1 ... WHEN 2 THRU 5 ... WHEN OTHER ... END-EVALUATE`
conditions.card.3: `EVALUATE TRUE` + `WHEN condition`: the first true one wins
conditions.card.4: `88 IS-RED VALUE "R".` then `IF IS-RED`, `SET IS-RED TO TRUE`

conditions-2.explain: `N < 5` is false for `5`. With `AND`, both conditions must be true, so the `ELSE` part runs.
conditions-3.explain: Both conditions are true, but `EVALUATE` runs only the first `WHEN` that matches.
conditions-4.statement: When several `WHEN` branches of an `EVALUATE` match, all of them run.
conditions-4.explain: Only the first matching `WHEN` runs. Then the program continues after `END-EVALUATE`.

conditions-5.explain: COBOL writes not equal as `NOT =`. The operator `!=` from other languages does not exist in COBOL.
conditions-6.prompt: Complete the code so it compiles and prints Even.
conditions-6.explain: `END-IF` closes an `IF`. COBOL writes it with a hyphen.
conditions-7.prompt: Build the statement that prints Big when TOTAL is greater than 100.
conditions-7.explain: The condition comes after `IF`, then the statement, and `END-IF` closes it.
conditions-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the code prints Positive when N is 3.
conditions-8.explain: The condition comes first, then the statements for true, `ELSE`, the statements for false, and `END-IF`.

conditions-10.explain: You set a condition name with `TRUE`: `SET IS-GREEN TO TRUE`. COBOL then moves `"G"` into `LIGHT`.
conditions-11.explain: The period ends the `IF` too early, so `ELSE` has no `IF` any more. Remove the period: `DISPLAY "Big"`.

loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat statements with PERFORM TIMES, count with PERFORM VARYING and loop until a condition is true with PERFORM UNTIL.
loops.lesson.0: `PERFORM` repeats statements. `PERFORM 3 TIMES` runs the statements up to `END-PERFORM` three times. Instead of a number you can also use a data item, for example `PERFORM ROUNDS TIMES`.
loops.lesson.3: `PERFORM VARYING I FROM 1 BY 1 UNTIL I > 5` uses `I` as a counter. It sets `I` to `1`, checks the condition before each round and adds `1` after each round. The loop stops as soon as the condition after `UNTIL` is true.
loops.lesson.5: `BY` sets the step. Here the loop adds the even numbers from `2` to `10`. A loop like this often builds a result, such as a total, in another data item.
loops.lesson.7: After the loop, the counter keeps the value that stopped it. After `UNTIL I > 5` with step `1`, `I` is `6`.
loops.lesson.9: `PERFORM UNTIL` repeats until a condition becomes true. It checks the condition **before** each round, so the body may not run at all. Make sure that the statements inside change something, or the loop never ends.
loops.lesson.11: With `WITH TEST AFTER`, COBOL checks the condition after each round instead. The body then always runs at least once.
loops.lesson.13: A counter needs enough digits. `PIC 9` holds at most `9`, so `9 + 1` becomes `0`, and `UNTIL I > 9` is never true. The loop then runs forever. Use `PIC 99` for a counter that must reach `10`.
loops.card.1: `PERFORM VARYING I FROM 1 BY 1 UNTIL I > 5 ... END-PERFORM`
loops.card.2: `PERFORM UNTIL X > 100 ... END-PERFORM` checks before each round
loops.card.3: `WITH TEST AFTER` checks after each round
loops.card.4: Give the counter enough digits, or the loop never ends

paragraphs.title: Paragraphs
paragraphs.summary: Split the PROCEDURE DIVISION into named paragraphs and run them with PERFORM.
paragraphs.lesson.0: Long programs are hard to read. A **paragraph** is a named group of statements in the `PROCEDURE DIVISION`. Its name stands on its own line and ends with a period. The paragraph ends with a period after its last statement.
paragraphs.lesson.1: `PERFORM GREET` runs the paragraph `GREET` and then comes back to the next statement. The first paragraph is the main part of the program, often called `MAIN-PARA`. It ends with `STOP RUN`, so the program does not run into the paragraphs below it.
paragraphs.lesson.3: All paragraphs use the same data items from `WORKING-STORAGE`. To give a paragraph input, move values into data items before the `PERFORM`. The paragraph leaves its result in a data item, too.
paragraphs.lesson.6: All forms of `PERFORM` from the last unit also work with a paragraph name. `PERFORM SHOW-LINE 3 TIMES` runs the paragraph three times. `PERFORM SHOW-ROW VARYING R FROM 1 BY 1 UNTIL R > 3` runs it once for each value of `R`. These forms have no `END-PERFORM`.
paragraphs.lesson.8: Without `STOP RUN`, the program does not stop at the end of the main paragraph. It goes on with the next paragraph, so that paragraph runs one extra time.
paragraphs.lesson.10: `PERFORM STEP-1 THRU STEP-3` runs all paragraphs from `STEP-1` to `STEP-3` in the order in which they appear in the code, and then comes back.
paragraphs.lesson.12: Give each paragraph one clear task and a name that says what it does, such as `PRINT-TOTAL` or `READ-NEXT`. Then `MAIN-PARA` reads like a table of contents.
paragraphs.card.0: `NAME.` on its own line starts a paragraph; a period ends it
paragraphs.card.1: `PERFORM NAME` runs it and comes back
paragraphs.card.3: `PERFORM A THRU C` runs A to C in order
paragraphs.card.4: End the main paragraph with `STOP RUN.`

tables.title: Tables
tables.summary: Store many values under one name with OCCURS, reach them with subscripts and process them in loops.
tables.lesson.0: A **table** holds many values of the same kind under one name. Other languages call it an array. You create one with `OCCURS`: `05 TEMP PIC 99 OCCURS 3 TIMES` makes three items called `TEMP`. Put the table inside a group item, here `TEMPS`, so that you can also use all elements together.
tables.lesson.1: A **subscript** in parentheses picks one element: `TEMP(1)` is the first, `TEMP(3)` the last. COBOL starts counting at `1`, not at `0`.
tables.lesson.3: The subscript can also be a data item, such as `TEMP(I)`. Together with `PERFORM VARYING`, this lets one loop visit every element.
tables.lesson.6: A group with a table can get a `VALUE` with all elements written one after another. Here `"254012"` fills three prices with two digits each: `25`, `40` and `12`. A loop then adds them up and finds the largest one.
tables.lesson.8: `INITIALIZE` resets a whole table at once: number items become zero and text items become spaces.
tables.lesson.10: `OCCURS` also works on a group. Each element then has several parts. `FRUIT-NAME(2)` is the name in the second element, and `FRUIT-QTY(2)` is its quantity.
tables.lesson.12: Keep every subscript between `1` and the size of the table. GnuCOBOL does not check this by default, so `TEMP(4)` in a table of three reads or changes memory that belongs to other data items.
tables.card.0: `05 TEMP PIC 99 OCCURS 3 TIMES.` inside an `01` group
tables.card.1: `TEMP(1)` is the first element, `TEMP(I)` element number I
tables.card.2: Loop over a table with `PERFORM VARYING I FROM 1 BY 1 UNTIL I > 3`
tables.card.3: `01 T VALUE "102030".` fills `05 N PIC 99 OCCURS 3.`
tables.card.4: `INITIALIZE T` sets numbers to zero, text to spaces

strings.title: Text handling
strings.summary: Cut, join, split and change text with reference modification, STRING, UNSTRING, INSPECT and text functions.
strings.lesson.0: Text items have a fixed size and are filled with spaces. COBOL has **intrinsic functions** that help: you write `FUNCTION`, the name and the input in parentheses. `FUNCTION TRIM` removes the spaces at both ends, and `FUNCTION UPPER-CASE` and `FUNCTION LOWER-CASE` change the letters.
strings.lesson.3: **Reference modification** takes a part of a text: `WORD(start:length)`. `WORD(1:4)` gives the first four characters, `WORD(5:3)` three characters from position `5`. Positions start at `1`. Without a length, as in `WORD(5:)`, you get the rest of the text.
strings.lesson.6: `STRING` joins several pieces `INTO` one item. Each piece has a `DELIMITED BY` phrase: `DELIMITED BY SIZE` takes the whole piece, and `DELIMITED BY SPACE` takes it only up to the first space. `STRING` does not clear the target, so `MOVE SPACES` to it first. `SPACES` stands for as many spaces as the item needs.
strings.lesson.8: `UNSTRING` does the opposite: it splits a text at a delimiter and puts the parts into several items, from left to right.
strings.lesson.11: `INSPECT ... TALLYING N FOR ALL "s"` counts how often `"s"` appears and adds the count to `N`. `INSPECT ... REPLACING ALL "s" BY "z"` replaces every `"s"` with `"z"`. Both texts must have the same length.
strings.lesson.13: `TALLYING` adds to the counter and does not reset it. Give the counter the start value `0`, or `MOVE 0` to it before every new count.

strings.card.3: `UNSTRING T DELIMITED BY "," INTO A B C`
strings.card.4: `INSPECT T TALLYING N FOR ALL "a"` / `REPLACING ALL "a" BY "o"`
strings-1.explain: `WORD(1:4)` takes four characters, starting at position `1`.
strings-2.explain: Position `4` is the `P`. From there, three characters give `PUT`.
strings-3.explain: `STRING` puts the three pieces directly one after another, without extra spaces.
strings-4.explain: `banana` has three `a`. `HITS` has two digits, so it prints `03`.
strings-5.statement: `STRING` fills the rest of the target item with spaces.
strings-5.explain: `STRING` changes only the characters it writes. The rest keeps its old content, so clear the target with `MOVE SPACES` first.
strings-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints red, then blue.
strings-6.explain: The delimiter is the text `","` in quotes. `UNSTRING` splits at each comma.
strings-7.prompt: Complete the code so it prints bonono.
strings-7.explain: `REPLACING ALL "a" BY "o"` changes every `a` into an `o`.
strings-8.prompt: Build the statement that copies CITY up to the first space into OUT-TEXT.
strings-8.explain: `DELIMITED BY SPACE` stops at the first space, and `INTO` names the target.
strings-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the code prints 17.05.2024.
strings-9.explain: Fill `DATE-TEXT` first, then split it, and print the parts at the end.
strings-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
strings-11.explain: Positions start at `1`, not `0`. Write `WORD(1:3)` for the first three characters.
strings-12.prompt: The code should print New York!. Which line has the bug?
strings-12.explain: `DELIMITED BY SPACE` stops at the space in `New York`. Use `DELIMITED BY SIZE` to take the whole item.
